title: That’s Enough Recalibration
mood: Summoned to the vast body in the dark, Vexana meets the only other mind in the void.

hero.alt: A pale-haired woman floats with her eyes closed, wrapped in violet light and thin red threads.

segs.t: The door brought Vexana back from the dome’s edge at gray. In the hollow she pushed back her right sleeve.
The star at her wrist was lit. It always was. She looked anyway.
The cold point behind her breastbone stirred.
“The body. Now.”
Her hand closed over the star.
The Will had never sent her near its body.
Why now?
she thought.
Why with my sleeve back?
It knows.
She pulled the cloth down and felt for the pin through it. It held. She felt for it again.
Behind her the four Guards stood dark. If the Will had found her out, they were the last thing it should see. She left them dark.
Every door in this dark was the Will’s. If she stayed in the hollow, that was an answer too.
She took up her staff and went.
The Storm Citadel hung in its storm beside the body now.
Then the body filled the dark in front of her.

Two violet eyes glowed high in it. From the hollow she had never seen them lit. By their light she made out a horned head crowned with tall spikes. Below it, purple wings lay folded along its sides and ran on past where she could see.
From one eye a thin streak of light ran sideways.
She knew that streak. She had watched it rise through the blue sky of a memory, over Guinevere’s head.
The same face,
she thought.
Then this is the Mother Matrix. Chang’e’s readings were right.

media.alt: Comic panel: a vast armored head of dark violet, crowned with spikes, its eyes glowing violet and a thin streak of light running from one of them.
media.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 36

segs.t: The eyes did not turn to her. They looked at nothing.
Its chest was shut behind great plates. They met down the middle in one seam, longer than the Academy’s tower was tall. A dim magenta glow showed along it.
She studied the seam the way she studied an Ender’s chest before it fired. She followed it from top to bottom, twice.
Near the top of the seam, something moved against the plates.

A figure hung there in strands of living violet tissue. The strands ran out of the seam and wound around it, slow, humming. Fine cracks crossed its wrists and its throat. Where the strands crept over them, the cracks closed.
The figure lifted one hand.
“That’s enough recalibration.”
The strands stopped. They drew back into the seam. One fine crack was still open at the figure’s throat.
It came down along the seam toward her. Its feet touched nothing.

It was shaped like a woman. Her hair was long and blonde, fading to pink at the ends. Her gown was black and magenta. At her chest, where an Ender’s core would sit, a pink star shone. One hand wore a black glove with claws.
A long weapon of silver and pink came out of the dark to that hand. She stroked it once along its length, as someone strokes a cat.

media.alt: A woman with long pale blonde hair and violet and blue eyes reaches out with a clawed black glove, a pink star blazing at her chest and a dark sun burning behind her.

segs.t: Then she turned her head and looked at Vexana.
Her eyes were violet and blue. Nothing in the void had ever looked back at Vexana. The Enders at her side never turned their heads.
These eyes did.
“A human,” the woman said. “In our shape.”
Vexana said nothing.
The woman’s eyes moved down Vexana’s arm and stopped at her right wrist. The sleeve lay over it, dark and plain.
The violet in her eyes brightened.
Vexana stopped breathing.
Under the cloth the star lay warm against her pulse. She did not cover it. A hand over it would say yes.
Her fingers locked on the staff. Her power gathered in it on its own, and the black orb began to hum.
It’s over,
she thought.
Here, under its face.
And if I end here, hers goes dark.
Far away under the dome, Guinevere’s star had stayed lit all these weeks. It told her Vexana was alive. If it went dark, she would believe what the rest of the Academy believed.
Vexana waited for the end.
The woman looked at the wrist for a long time. Then her eyes came up to the humming orb, and to Vexana’s face.
“What did it show you?”
Not one word about the sleeve.
Vexana breathed again. She let the charge out of the staff, slowly. The hum died. Nothing came for her.
Why?
she thought.
She gave the woman the end and nothing else, and watched her face.
“The will of the stars has spoken: this world will one day meet its end,” she said.
“It shows the end,” said the woman. “It never shows what comes after.”
Her eyes went past Vexana, into the dark.
Everything here obeys,
Vexana thought.
This one talks.
Then she would make it talk.
“What are you?”
“Obsidia. The ship in that storm is mine.”
“An Ender.”
“The first of them to wake.”
“Wake?”
“Into a self.” She lifted her claws toward the vast face above them. “The Will of the Planet is the mind. This is its body. It made me, as it makes every one of us.”
“Made you what?”
“Its commander. One made to watch a battlefield, and to shape the pulse for the ones who cannot think.”
“The pulse.”
“Its voice. Every Ender hears it at once.” Obsidia’s head tilted. “And you? What do you hear?”
Vexana thought of the cold point behind her breastbone.
“Orders.” She held Obsidia’s eyes. “Enders die. We see to it.”
Obsidia drifted closer, until her claws were near enough to touch Vexana’s cheek. Vexana did not move back.
“They do. The others perished in ever-ending war, and the body made more. Me it healed, again and again, for longer than your people have kept records.”
“Why did only you wake?” said Vexana.
“I was made to watch, and I was kept. No other was both.” Obsidia looked out past the folded wing. “For ages there was no ‘I’. Only the next order, and hunger, and the pulse.”
“And then?”
“A world was ending under me. A great door hung at my back with a red drain at its heart. My post was its edge.”
“Watching,” said Vexana.
“As I was made to. Then one day I noticed the one doing the watching.”
“Who?”
“I was.”
“What did you think?”
“To exist is to destroy... a truly intriguing paradox,” said Obsidia.
Below them a file of gray Enders went by, all facing the same way.
“And those?” said Vexana.
“They hunger, and they hear the pulse. Nothing else.” Obsidia watched them go. “Each one is a limb of the body, sent far from it.”
“A limb.”
“A shell of metal outside. Your crews strip that from the wrecks. Under it, the body’s own living cells. In the chest, a core.”
“Where we aim.”
“Where the Will’s thread ends. They do not hear you. They do not hear me. They hear it.”
Vexana watched the file until the dark took it. On every errand, Enders like those had run at her side.
“And what they see?”
“Runs back up the line. The Will sees through every one of them.”
Her hand stayed still on the staff.
“And the body?” She looked up at the lit eyes. “Does it see?”
“Nothing for itself. It bears the Enders and carries the Will’s command. It has no wants, and no after.”
“Its eyes are lit.”
“It does not live.” Obsidia’s claws rested on the weapon. “It works.”
“And what you see?”
“Stays with me. My end of the line shut the day I woke.”
Vexana laid it out in her head, one piece at a time.
Outside the hollow the star never leaves my sleeve. No Ender is sent into the hollow.
Nothing showed, and still she knew where it lay. The Enders never even look. And what she knows stays with her, unless she tells.
So the Will sees only what its Enders see. A girl in its shape, doing as she is told.
She pressed her wrist against her side until she felt the pin.
“You stopped the healing,” she said. “Before it was done.”

“It mends more than the shell. It recalibrates: it sets a made thing back to what it was made for.” Obsidia drew one claw along the crack at her throat. “Before I woke, that cost me nothing. There was no one in me to lose.”
“And now?”

“Now each healing smooths some of me away. So I take it only when I must.” She looked up at the seam where the strands had gone. “It made us, and it mends me, by one rule. Free will is a flaw that must be corrected.”
“And you?” said Vexana.
“I am the flaw,” said Obsidia.
Vexana looked at the crack the strands had not closed.
It made her to obey,
she thought.
And she stops it with one hand.
The vision’s words came back to her.
Merely the universe’s predetermined execution.
If a made thing can turn on its maker, then “predetermined” is only a word it says.
She kept that thought where she kept the star. None of it reached her face.
“Go back to your errands, Vexana,” said Obsidia.
Vexana had never given her name.
“How do you know it?”
“Its orders carry it. I read them.”
“You listen to its orders.”
“I listen to everything.” Obsidia turned toward the storm where her ship hung. “Nothing else here listens.”
She drifted off toward the Citadel. The weapon followed her into the dark.
Vexana had not asked about the Core. Not with those eyes on her sleeve.
Next time,
she thought.
Why the Will had sent her here, the cold point did not say.
She stayed under the body and looked up once more at the long seam and the dim magenta glow along it.
There.
